system_map.overview: The system is a Python-based governance and evaluation runner (cas_runner) designed to manage architecture knowledge, enforce governance rules, and evaluate agent skills. It exhibits a layered architecture with clear separation between CLI, orchestration, domain services, and infrastructure adapters. Core modules group around governance, LLM integration, skills evaluation, and health monitoring. The system leverages Pydantic for domain modeling, uses adapter patterns for LLM clients, and employs a bootstrap process for workspace configuration.

patterns.name: Pydantic Governance Domain Models
patterns.summary: Use Pydantic BaseModel classes to represent governance entities, ensuring validation and serialization consistency.
patterns.intent: Provide a strongly typed, self-validating domain layer for governance data.
patterns.context: The governance module requires structured representation of inventories, health statuses, compliance findings, and actions. Data flows from external sources into these models for processing and persistence.
forces: Need for validation of incoming data from varied sources.
Serialization to JSON or other formats for persistence and communication.
Flexibility to evolve models as governance rules change.
patterns.solution: Define all governance data structures as Pydantic models with explicit field types and validators. These models serve as the canonical schema throughout the codebase.
implementation_signals: Classes in governance/models.py: GovernanceInventory, GovernanceHealth, ComplianceFinding, GovernanceAction, etc.

evidence.note: Central location for all governance-related data structures.

benefits: Early validation errors reduce runtime failures.
Clear contracts for data exchange between components.
Easy generation of JSON schemas for documentation.
costs: Potential performance overhead for large datasets.
Learning curve for contributors unfamiliar with Pydantic.
failure_modes: Overly strict validation may reject legitimate data.
Model changes require updates in dependent services.

patterns.reuse_notes: Applicable to any module requiring structured data representations.

extraction_metadata.evidence_basis: Direct symbol analysis from models.py and project dependencies.

patterns.name: Transition Registry for State Machines
patterns.summary: Utilize a registry to define allowed state transitions and actions for governance workflows.
patterns.intent: Enable flexible evolution of governance actions without hardcoding transition logic.
patterns.context: GovernanceActionEngine likely orchestrates state transitions between governance phases (e.g., from review to decision). TransitionRegistry holds the mapping of current state and event to resulting action.
forces: Need to add new transition types without modifying core engine.
Ensure only valid transitions are executed.
Provide a declarative way to define workflow rules.
patterns.solution: Maintain a TransitionRegistry that maps (from_state, event) to (to_state, action). The engine queries this registry to determine next steps and execute the associated action.
implementation_signals: GovernanceActionEngine likely uses this registry internally.

evidence.note: Registry pattern embedded in state machine logic.

benefits: Easy to add new transitions and rules.
Testability: transitions can be unit-tested independently.
costs: Registry must be kept in sync with actual logic.
Complexity for very large state spaces.
failure_modes: Missing transitions leading to runtime errors.
Registry becoming a god object if not partitioned.

patterns.reuse_notes: Ideal for any workflow engine with discrete states and events.

extraction_metadata.evidence_basis: Symbol names in governance_action_engine.py indicate registry-based transition management.

patterns.name: LLM Client Adapter
patterns.summary: Provide a common interface for LLM access, with concrete implementations for different providers.
patterns.intent: Decouple application code from specific LLM providers, enabling swapping and testing.
patterns.context: The system uses LiteLLM for real calls and a mock client for testing. Both must conform to the same interface so that the rest of the code can depend on an abstraction.
forces: Need to support multiple LLM providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) via LiteLLM.
Testing without incurring costs or external dependencies.
Maintain flexibility to switch providers.
patterns.solution: Define a common interface (e.g., chat_completion method) and implement LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient. The rest of the system uses the interface, allowing dependency injection.
implementation_signals: LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient classes in llm/ directory.
Both likely implement a shared method like generate or complete.

benefits: Unit tests can use mock client.
costs: Interface must capture all needed operations.
failure_modes: Mock client may not perfectly simulate real behavior.

patterns.reuse_notes: Classic adapter pattern, applicable to any external service.

extraction_metadata.evidence_basis: Two client classes observed in key files; project uses LiteLLM library.

patterns.name: Layered Module Boundaries
patterns.summary: Organize code into clear layers: CLI, orchestration, domain models, and infrastructure adapters.
patterns.intent: Promote separation of concerns and maintainability.
patterns.context: The repository structure groups related functionality: cli.py for entry, runner.py for flow, governance/ for services, llm/ for adapters, skills/ for evaluation models, dashboard/ for health reporting.
forces: Need to evolve components independently.
Minimize dependencies across layers.
Make testing easier by isolating each layer.
patterns.solution: Define module boundaries based on responsibility: presentation (CLI), application (runner/services), domain (models), and infrastructure (llm, bootstrap). Enforce dependency rules where higher layers depend on lower ones, not vice versa.
implementation_signals: Top-level directories: cli.py, runner.py, governance/, llm/, skills/, dashboard/.
Each module exposes a limited public API.

benefits: Easier to test each layer in isolation.
costs: May lead to over-abstraction if too many layers.
failure_modes: Layers may become blurred if services leak into models.

patterns.reuse_notes: Typical for Python projects using package organization.

extraction_metadata.evidence_basis: Directory structure and key file grouping.

patterns.intent: Enable modular and composable configuration without overwriting user-specific settings.
patterns.context: The bootstrap process merges CAS governance blocks and Claude settings, likely to allow user configs to overlay defaults.
forces: User configurations may need to be preserved.
Default configurations should be applied.
Merge must handle conflicts predictably.
patterns.solution: Implement merge functions that combine dictionaries or YAML structures, giving precedence to user-defined settings while applying system defaults.

evidence.note: Specific merge functions for configuration blocks.

costs: Merge logic can become complex for nested structures.
Need to handle null/empty values gracefully.
failure_modes: Merging may produce invalid configurations if not properly validated.

patterns.reuse_notes: Common in tools that generate and modify workspace configurations.

extraction_metadata.evidence_basis: Function names directly indicate merging of governance and Claude settings.

patterns.name: Evaluation Suite Models
patterns.summary: Define structured models for test cases, suites, and results to standardize evaluation.
patterns.intent: Provide a reusable framework for defining and reporting skill evaluations.
patterns.context: skills/models.py contains EvalStatus, SkillAssertions, SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalResult, SkillEvalReport. These capture the essential entities for evaluation workflows.
forces: Need consistent formatting of evaluation cases.
Results need to be aggregated and reported.
Allow new assertion types.
patterns.solution: Use Pydantic models to represent evaluation semantics, with fields for inputs, assertions, outcomes, and metadata.
implementation_signals: Classes like SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite in skills/models.py.

costs: May be over-engineered for simple evaluations.
failure_modes: Overly rigid models hinder innovative evaluation techniques.
Missing fields may cause compatibility issues.

patterns.reuse_notes: Reusable in any testing framework requiring structured test definitions.

extraction_metadata.evidence_basis: Numerous model classes define evaluation domain.

anti_patterns.name: Centralized Models God Module
symptoms: All governance models in one file (models.py) increasing in size.
Many classes in a single module, potentially hundreds of lines.
impact: Higher merge conflicts and difficulty in understanding dependencies.
suggested_remediation: Split models into submodules based on aggregate boundaries (e.g., health_models.py, compliance_models.py).
Use package-level __init__.py to re-export for backward compatibility.

anti_patterns.name: Tight Coupling Between Service and Engine
symptoms: GovernanceActionService directly instantiates GovernanceActionEngine without injection.
Engine and service are in same package and likely intimately linked.
impact: Changes in engine may require updates in service.
suggested_remediation: Use dependency injection to pass engine instances.
